title: MCP 2026: New Specification & Ecosystem Growth
content:
## Overview

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has grown substantially since its November 2024 launch. By mid-2026 the ecosystem spans over 500 public servers, a forthcoming major specification update, and a shift from reference implementations toward vendor-operated and community-maintained servers.

---

## MCP 2026 Specification: Release Candidate

A release candidate for the next major MCP specification is available as of mid-2026, with the final release expected on **July 28, 2026**. Key changes:

### Stateless Protocol Core
The core protocol is redesigned to be stateless by default, simplifying server implementation and enabling horizontal scaling without session affinity. Stateful behaviors — streaming, subscriptions — are moved to an opt-in **Extensions** framework.

### Extensions Framework
Optional protocol capabilities are formalized as Extensions. Servers declare which extensions they support; clients negotiate at connection time. This replaces ad-hoc capability negotiation from earlier versions and makes the protocol forward-compatible without breaking existing servers.

### Tasks Primitive
**Tasks** are a new first-class concept: long-running, interruptible units of work that a server executes on behalf of a client. A Task has an ID, a status (`pending` / `running` / `completed` / `failed`), and produces streamed output. This enables patterns like "start a background job, poll for completion, retrieve result" without holding a long-lived connection open.

### MCP Apps
**MCP Apps** are packaged bundles of a prompt + tools + resources that can be installed by a user and invoked by name. They allow distributing complete agent capabilities — not just raw tools — through the MCP ecosystem, similar to how browser extensions bundle functionality.

### Authorization Hardening
The spec adds formal **OAuth 2.1** support for remote servers and clarifies permission scoping, addressing security concerns with the original authorization model where some servers required overly broad token grants.

### Formal Deprecation Policy
The 2026 spec introduces an explicit deprecation policy: protocol features will have a minimum 12-month deprecation window with documented migration paths, giving the broader ecosystem time to adapt before breaking changes ship.

---

## Ecosystem Scale: 500+ Servers

As of early 2026, over 500 public MCP servers are available, up from the initial handful at launch. The community adds new servers weekly. Major categories:

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| Databases | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB |
| File Storage | Google Drive, Box, Dropbox, S3 |
| Code & Dev | GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Linear |
| Messaging | Slack, email, Discord |
| Web | Brave Search, Puppeteer, Playwright |
| Finance | Stripe, SEC filing data |
| Productivity | Asana, Notion, Google Calendar |

The community-maintained registry at `github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers` remains the primary discovery point.

---

## Vendor Migration of Reference Servers

A significant ecosystem shift: most of Anthropic's original first-party reference servers — for GitHub, filesystem, PostgreSQL, and others — were **archived during 2025** and migrated to vendor or community ownership. The upstream repo now maintains a smaller curated set with explicit pointers to actively maintained forks.

This reflects ecosystem maturity: vendors now take responsibility for their own integrations rather than depending on Anthropic-maintained stubs. It also means integration quality has generally improved, as vendors have stronger incentives to keep their own MCP servers current.

---

## Remote MCP: HTTP/SSE Transport in Production

While stdio transport remains common for local development, **remote MCP** via HTTP + Server-Sent Events (SSE) has become the standard for production deployments. Remote servers:

- Run independently of the client machine
- Can be shared across a team
- Support authentication and audit logging
- Enable SaaS-style MCP integrations

Several major cloud providers now offer managed MCP server hosting, making it straightforward to deploy a private MCP server without managing infrastructure.

---

## MCP in Claude Code Sessions

Claude Code connects to MCP servers via its settings file. As of 2026, the most commonly used MCP servers in Claude Code sessions are the GitHub server (for PR reviews, issue triage), filesystem extensions, and search providers. The session-level MCP tool listing (shown in `<system-reminder>` messages) reflects servers connected at session start.

For production Claude Code environments, teams configure a curated set of MCP servers in `.claude/settings.json` committed to the repo, so every session starts with the same tool surface.
